Essential revisions:

1) The report needs to make clear what are the novel findings.

2) How did differences in cell counts and other measures of injection site affect the pattern and extent of anterogradely labelled cell and mossy fibre terminals? It was not clear to me if Figure 2A shows the total extent of injection sites into different neocortical areas or just the defined regions of interest. Either way the area clearly varies considerably between targets which will affect projection density and possibly topography.

3) The histogram axes in Figure 2D are not all drawn on the same scale making comparisons difficult. Also percentage values are potentially misleading given the large variation in cell counts and mossy fibre terminals listed in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

4) Given that the pons is the primary source of mossy fibre inputs, how did the authors determine that other brainstem nuclei also containing labelled cells in the same experiments necessarily provided mossy fibre projections?

5) The topographical organization within the pons should be compared to the principles of organization defined in previous studies (eg Leergaard, 2003; Odeh et al., 2005).

6) The discussion should consider the extent to which cerebro-cerebellar pathways are conserved across mammalian species. How useful is the mouse as a model for study of cerebro-cerebellar projections?

Reviewer #3:

Henschke and Pakan have submitted a manuscript entitled "Convergence of multimodal inputs connecting the cerebral cortex to the cerebellum" in which they use modern neuronal tracing methods to map circuit projections into the mouse cerebellum. The authors traced the cerebellar inputs originating from sensory, motor, and association cortices. They argue that diverse functional connections project from the cortex to cerebellum, where they ultimately exhibit a convergent terminal field distribution within specific lobules. The manuscript is well written and technically, it offers a much-needed approach to better understand the organization and trajectories of major cortico-cerebellar projections. In addition, the figures are well made, schematics very helpful, and overall the panels are easy to follow. However, below we provide a number of comments and concerns that we hope will improve the clarity and impact of the study.

1) Throughout the text, the discussion of A1 and its unique projection through non-pontine pre-cerebellar nuclei is often highlighted, however the significance of this point is not well articulated. Further clarification in the abstract and in the body is needed if the authors wish to highlight the uniqueness of this pathway. This is especially true given the findings in the text that S1 and M1 both have substantial, if not even majority in the case of S1, projections to non-pontine pre-cerebellar nuclei.

2) Introduction. Please clarify why the identified cortical regions were selected. In addition, while we agree that the characterization of the injections is rather comprehensive, there is a limitation in this study in that either the number of cortical regions chosen or the breadth of the characterization of the selected regions (ie: why weren't at least two neighboring sites in a given cortical region analyzed) prevent the present study from providing a fully comprehensive map, as stated by the authors.

3) Figure 1A. Please indicate the circumscribed subregion in each cortical area where the injection was made.

4) Subsection “Anterograde tracing of indirect cerebrocerebellar pathways”. Please clarify percentages for A1 projections in order to make the second sentence "This pattern of extra-pontine labeling was similar…" clearer. Further, in Figure 2B, while the scarcity of the projections to the pontine nuclei is similar, they seem to be qualitatively different in that A1 projects terminals, while the AuD experiment labels cell bodies. This distinction is not clear in the text. Moreover, the fact you see terminals in one region and then cell bodies another makes it a challenge to piece together what the actual pathway(s) might look like. That is, how do you substantiate the claim that the cell bodies in the pons (the unexpected labeling) actually project to the cerebellum? And on the flip side, for the majority of S1 labeling, which is in the precerebellar non-pontine nuclei, can we really assume that these all project to cerebellum? If not, what percentage?

5) The Supplementary file 1 is a bit difficult to interpret. Please include the percentages referenced in the text in the table. In addition, it is unclear why in some injection sites the sum of the individual pre-cerebellar nuclei cells equals the summed total, while in other cases the sum is less than or greater than the listed total. (ie M1-1 52 vs 55; V1-1 8 vs 8; A1-1 10 vs 8)

6) The significance of terminals in pontine/pre-cerebellar nuclei without cell body labelling is unclear and there should be an explanation of this in the text. For instance, in regard to A1/AuD does this indicate inefficiency in trans-synaptic labelling, that there is an alternative monosynaptic projection from A1/AuD to the pontine nuclei, or is there an alternative explanation? This is mentioned for M1 projections to the olivary nuclei (Subsection “Anterograde tracing of indirect cerebrocerebellar pathways”).

7) In the subsection "Convergence of multimodal cerebrocerebellar input within lobules…" the metric for dominant representation (> or < 55%) is problematic given the relative sparsity of the injections (either across or within cortical regions). Furthermore, given the variability of numbered terminals across individual animals in a given cortical area (ie from 2406 to 25616 from the M1 injections), this type of quantification and conclusions about convergence seem premature.

8) While the discussion about convergence and integration is quite interesting to speculate upon, it is hard to grasp whether the current data is sufficient to reach such a conclusion. Given the vast number of granule cells and the fine scale nature of cerebellar microzones, conclusions about integration of multimodal afferent information by single units (whether microzone or granule cell) cannot be easily drawn. To do this, a method distinct from the approach used in this paper would be needed whereby labelling from two distinct cortical areas could be distinguished in the cerebellum in a single animal. In the end, I am having trouble fully appreciating how integrated the "multimodal" and "convergence" nature of the pathways actually is, based on the data provided.

9) Finally, there is a core assumption at play, which is that cortical injection - pontine/precerebellar cell body labeling - mossy fiber terminal marking. In the case of cortico-ponto-cerebellar pathways, the abundance of literature makes this assumption sound. However, in the case of the precerebellar projections (especially S1 which has a majority non-pontine projections), sagittal sections (for example) demonstrating the axonal projections, and elucidating the monosynaptic pathway would provide a helpful piece of evidence to support the current content.

1) In the Abstract, it is not clear what is actually meant by "Prominent terminal overlap across motor and sensory modalities…". And, how was this measured?

2) It would be very helpful to include the species studied in the Title and/or the Abstract.

3) It is critical that the authors fully outline the limitations of the mono-trans synaptic anterograde viral tracer, in their hands, and specifically for the purpose of this study.

4) In Figure 1B, it is not clear what the red arrows are representing and pointing towards. Aren't the arrows pointing the wrong way if this is to show anterograde tracing direction?

5) Is there a time dependence on the tracing? That is, do longer periods of survival after injection label additional projections?

6) In Figure 1F, M1 should project ipsilateral, but in the cerebellum one can see many terminals on both sides. Please explain.

7) The authors state "…extent M1, indicating the presence of a polysynaptic cerebro-olivary pathway…" What is the literature to support this?

8) The authors state "We quantified the number of resulting mossy fiber terminals throughout the extent of the cerebellum and found that this was highly variable across cortical regions…" How variable is the size of the infected cell population in the cortex?

9) The authors state "There was a clear and consistent topography of…" It would be helpful to fully define what you mean by topography here. There are many levels of topography, in different brain regions, and this could mean very different things to different researchers.

10) In Figure 3E, what does each data point represent? A single terminal?

11) Along the same lines as above, it would be helpful to see more actual data with the combined zebrin labeling. Mossy fiber patterns, by nature of their clustered appearance, are not so easily appreciated and therefore additional examples, at higher power magnification, would be welcomed.

12) The authors state "This allowed for a detailed comparison of cerebellar regions across brains and, hence, across functional cortical regions representing multiple modalities (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1)." However, I don't see a full description or explanation of the data in the text.

13) The number of animals used in the study seems quite low.

14) In Figure 3—figure supplement 1, what is the red staining in Purkinje cells?

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Cerebral cortical connections to the cerebellum across multiple modalities" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been evaluated by Richard Ivry (Senior Editor) and a Reviewing Editor.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below:

Summary:

Henschke and Pakan have provided a substantially revised version of a paper describing the connectivity between different areas of the cerebral cortex with the cerebellum. The authors have used a virus based transsynaptic tracing approach to show that multi-modal inputs may converge upon specific topographical domains within the cerebellar vermis and hemispheres. The study is anatomical in nature and takes an in-depth analysis of mossy fiber terminal field distributions in the cerebellum, but the authors also examine the different intermediate projections of the cerebral-cerebellar projections that are located within various brainstem nuclei. The paper is well-written and the images are high quality. reviewers particularly appreciated the addition of important controls (characterization of extra-pontine sources of MFs, confirmation of pontine sources using retrograde labeling, and identification of an A1-colliculo-cerebellar pathway), which significantly increase confidence in their original findings and propel the study towards the authors' original objective as a seminal reference, or atlas, for the characterization of cerebrocerebellar mossy fiber (MF) pathways.

Essential revisions:

The major remaining concern – shared by both reviewers – is the overemphasis/ speculation on 'multimodality' for this essentially anatomical study. Specifically:

1) I was delighted to see a more detailed examination of the location of MFs from different modalities within each lobule, since a prerequisite for multimodal processing is that the information project to the same subregion of a lobule. I also found rather striking the case in Crus II where there was still segregation between two MF types within the same lobe. This latter result highlights the notion that multimodal innervation within lobes is necessary but not sufficient to conclude multimodal processing. I therefore encourage the authors to soften their choice of words of "highly multimodal" and "moderately multimodal" as a conclusion of Figure 4. Perhaps the use of the term "lobule co-innervation" is more appropriate. Then after Figure 5, the argument for putative multimodal processing is much stronger, but still only suggestive.

2) Indeed, Figure 5 shows an essential set of analyses suggestive of multimodal processing, but I was left wanting for some clear quantification of "intermingled" and a simple overall summary.

a) Would it be possible to analyze the distribution of nearest-neighbor distances between terminals of different origins? Those that co-innervate would have shorter distances and those that do not, e.g. Crus II, would show a shifted distribution. Perhaps a more sophisticated point-process analysis, such as the application of the bivariate Ripley K-function, could be used to test for spatial randomness between two species of points and provide statistical confidence.

b) To add some statistical rigor to the alignment with adolase C staining, one could compare the frequency of AldoC positive and negative terminals for each cortical injection. Statistical tests for the frequency of events can then be used.

3) The title continues to hint at a more functional set of analyses, which the paper really does not provide. Please revise.

4) Similarly, the Abstract could present the key anatomical distinctions that were uncovered rather than the speculative discussion about multimodal sensory input – this functional idea should remain, but it should be toned down to make space to better clarify the actual anatomical findings.

5) The main Figure 6 merits a more thorough quantification of retrograde labeling.

6) Quantification and presentation of co-labeled and spatially intermingled neurons following dual viral tracing injections would be appropriate.

7) I like the estimation of the number of MFs per pontine neuron and would like to see it as a main figure.

8) The Discussion section rambles on a bit. I believe it can be shortened and used to more clearly summarize the major findings, the similarities and differences with previous results, and the implications for cerebellar function.

9) The section titles are rather vague. For example, "Organization of cerebrocerebellar mossy fiber terminals" is essentially duplicated in the Results and Discussion, and perhaps needs more specific wording. "Spatial organization of cerebrocerebellar mossy fiber types". I am not really sure why there is a Discussion subsection on "Diversity of cerebrocerebellar pathways" as you define the pathways by viral injection. Perhaps something like: "Cerebellar cortical target diversity of cerebrocerebellar pathways?"

results.result: The study confirms a highly organized topography of corticopontine projections in mice, with rostral cortical regions projecting medially and caudal regions projecting laterally in the pons. M1 was unique in showing bilateral pontine labeling, while other cortical regions showed strictly ipsilateral projections.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C32, C33, C41-C43 are directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1E and 3B, with quantification provided. The topographic organization is consistent with previous studies (C172, C173), providing cross-validation. The bilateral M1 projections are quantified (118±36 ipsilateral vs 8±3 contralateral neurons) with statistical support.

results.result: Primary auditory cortex (A1) showed no direct corticopontine pathway in mice, as demonstrated by absence of labeled pontine cells after A1 injections using both anterograde (AAV1.cre) and retrograde (CAV.cre) tracing methods.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C27, C28, C34, C35 are supported by converging evidence from two independent tracing methods (anterograde and retrograde), shown in Figures 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The absence of labeling is a negative result but is well-controlled and confirmed by multiple approaches (C177, C178, C184).

results.result: Multiple extra-pontine precerebellar nuclei receive direct cortical projections, with S1 and M1 showing substantial labeling in brainstem nuclei including red nucleus, reticulotegmental nucleus, spinal trigeminal nucleus, lateral reticular nucleus, matrix region x, and vestibular nuclei.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C49-C52, C200 are supported by anatomical observations in Figure 2A and quantification in Supplementary file 1B. The proportion of extra-pontine labeling is quantified for S1 (70±8%) and M1 (40±3%), providing strong quantitative support for the existence of these pathways.

results.result: Labeled fibers in the pons after A1 injections may represent either fibers of passage or disynaptic terminals from indirect pathways via the inferior colliculus. Anterograde labeling was consistently observed in the inferior colliculus after A1 injections, and IC injections produced pontine and cerebellar labeling, supporting a potential trisynaptic A1-IC-pontine-cerebellar pathway.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C40, C185-C186, C188-C189 are supported by experimental data in Figures 2B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2. The observation of labeled neurons in IC after A1 injections (C39) and subsequent pontine/cerebellar labeling after IC injections (C40) provides anatomical evidence for the proposed pathway. However, the interpretation involves some speculation (C37, C38, C188) about the nature of the fibers.

results.result: The cerebellar hemispheres were the major target of cerebrocerebellar mossy fiber terminals, receiving the majority of total input (68.2% ipsilateral, 67.1% contralateral). Projections were largely contralateral (average 70±3%), with S1 showing the strongest contralateral bias (85±3%).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C29, C69-C70, C74, C107, C215 are supported by comprehensive quantification data shown in Figures 3 and 4, with specific percentages provided for each cortical region. The data are internally consistent and based on systematic counting of mossy fiber terminals across all cerebellar lobules.

results.result: At least sparse cerebrocerebellar projections were found to every lobule of the cerebellum from motor and sensory cortices, with terminals spanning all regions of the cerebellar cortex. The proportion of terminals in each lobule varied widely (0.1-19.3% ipsilateral, 0.1-16.9% contralateral).
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C30, C105-C106, C216 are supported by quantification data in Figures 3D and 4A-B showing terminal distribution across all cerebellar lobules. The finding challenges traditional views of cerebellar organization and is well-documented with specific percentages for each lobule.

results.result: Cerebrocerebellar projections from association/secondary cortical regions (PPC, AuD) showed significantly less laterality than those from primary sensory and motor cortices, with the ratio of ipsilateral to contralateral terminals being 0.73±0.13 versus 0.35±0.06 respectively (p=0.008).
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C71, C90, C210 are supported by quantification data with statistical analysis (two-sample t-test, p=0.008). The finding is based on systematic comparison across cortical regions and is shown in Figure 3. The statistical test is appropriate for the comparison being made.

results.result: Spatial overlap of mossy fiber terminals from functionally distinct cortical areas occurs within crus I, paraflocculus, and vermal regions IV/V and VI, identifying these regions as potential hubs for multimodal cortical influence. All gross divisions of the cerebellar cortex have potential for cortical multimodal influence.
results.evaluation: Claims C9-C10, C31, C122, C225-C226 are supported by spatial analysis data in Figures 5 and 6, with quantification of terminal overlap from different cortical regions. The classification of 'highly co-innervated' regions is based on defined criteria (>4% total input, >15% from at least two functional regions). The spatial overlap is demonstrated through nearest-neighbor analysis and pairwise distance measurements.

results.result: In crus II, terminals from M1 and S1 were spatially segregated, with M1 terminals in dorsal regions and S1 in ventral regions. Statistical analysis showed M1 and S1 terminals were significantly closer to themselves than to terminals from other cortical origins (M1-M1: 258±22 µm vs M1-Other: 305±10 µm, p=0.007; S1-S1: 190±13 µm vs S1-Other: 316±15 µm, p<0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C126-C132 are supported by spatial mapping in Figure 5A and statistical analysis in Figure 5B-C. The pairwise distance measurements and nearest-neighbor analysis (>80% of M1 nearest neighbors were also M1) provide quantitative support for spatial segregation. The statistical tests (two-sample t-tests) are appropriate and show significant differences.

results.result: In crus I, PFl, and vermal lobules IV/V and VI, terminals from different cortical regions showed high spatial overlap. In crus I, M1 and S1 terminal distances to other cortical origins were not significantly different from distances to themselves. Terminals showed distinct apical/basal patterns in the PFl and medial/paravermal patterns in vermal lobules.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C141 are supported by spatial analysis in Figures 5B-C and 6A-B. The lack of significant difference in pairwise distances for crus I (C133) and the higher proportion of nearest neighbors from extrinsic origins (C134) support spatial overlap. The apical/basal and medial/paravermal patterns (C135-C141) are documented in the spatial reconstructions.

results.result: Since no pontine labeling was observed after A1 injections but mossy fiber terminals were present in the cerebellum, the disynaptic mossy fiber input from A1 must reach the cerebellum through extra-pontine precerebellar nuclei, with labeling found in vestibular and cochlear nuclei.
results.evaluation: Claims C56, C179, C205 represent a logical inference from the experimental observations: absence of pontine labeling (C4, C27) combined with presence of cerebellar terminals (C178) necessitates extra-pontine pathways. The observation of labeling in vestibular and cochlear nuclei (Figure 2A) provides anatomical support for this conclusion.

results.result: Retrograde tracing from cerebellar cortex showed the majority of labeled cells in the pons (73% pontine, 27% extra-pontine). Dual injections revealed double-labeled cells in pontine nuclei, confirming disynaptic cerebrocerebellar input. Extra-pontine precerebellar nuclei also showed spatially overlapping labeling, with 13-45% of nearest neighbors to anterogradely labeled cells being retrogradely labeled from cerebellum.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C165 are supported by retrograde tracing data in Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1. The observation of double-labeled cells (C160-C161) provides direct confirmation of disynaptic connectivity. The nearest-neighbor analysis (C165) quantifies the spatial overlap in extra-pontine nuclei, though the absence of directly observed double-labeled cells in these nuclei (C164) is noted.

results.result: A stronger positive correlation was found between total mossy fiber terminals and all precerebellar cells (R=0.837, p<0.001) compared to pontine cells only (R=0.632, p=0.012). Lower variability in mossy fibers per cell was found when including all precerebellar cells (50±12) versus pontine only (120±63).
results.evaluation: Claims C169-C170 are supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7D. The stronger correlation and lower variability when including extra-pontine cells suggest these pathways contribute significantly to cerebellar input. However, the analysis cannot precisely determine the proportion of terminals relaying through each pathway (C201), which is acknowledged as a limitation.

results.result: Fibers and terminal labeling were observed in the inferior olive following S1 injections and to a lesser extent after M1 injections. Anterogradely labeled cells were observed in matrix region x after S1 and M1 injections. The results support disynaptic input from cerebral cortex to inferior olivary neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60, C62 are supported by experimental observations in Figure 2C and anatomical data. The observation of fibers/terminals in the inferior olive (C58-C59) and labeled cells in matrix region x (C60), which has been suggested as a preolivary relay nucleus, support the inference of disynaptic input (C62). However, the interpretation involves inference from anatomical connectivity rather than direct functional demonstration.

results.result: S1 injections resulted in patchy distribution of mossy fiber terminals that aligned with AldoC expression patterns in some lobules (especially Cop and PM with AldoC+ stripes, crus I with AldoC- bias), though distributed labeling was also present in both AldoC+ and AldoC- regions. Statistical analysis showed significant deviation from complete spatial randomness in most lobules except crus II and lobule IV.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C147, C149-C151 are supported by spatial mapping in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and statistical analysis using Ripley's K-function. The patchy distribution and alignment with AldoC patterns in specific lobules (C146-C147) is documented, though the relationship is not strict (C149-C150). The statistical test for spatial randomness (C151) is appropriate and shows significant clustering in most lobules.

results.result: M1 terminals showed a more distributed, less clustered pattern that did not consistently follow AldoC expression boundaries, though still deviated significantly from complete spatial randomness in most lobules (except lobule VI). Other cortical regions showed distributed/sparse labeling that only deviated from spatial randomness in specific lobules. Overall, mono-trans-synaptic terminals did not adhere to a specific pattern of zonal organization with respect to AldoC boundaries.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C157 are supported by spatial mapping data and statistical analysis using Ripley's K-function. The lack of consistent alignment with AldoC boundaries (C152, C154, C156) is documented, though significant deviation from spatial randomness is still observed (C153, C155, C157). The conclusion (C156) appropriately acknowledges that finer-scale relationships may exist (C158).

results.result: The number of mossy fiber terminals was highly variable across cortical regions (S1 and M1: ~10,000; AuD: ~580), but the regional pattern of labeling was highly consistent within and specific to each cortical region injected.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C68 are supported by quantification data in Supplementary file 1B and Figure 3. The variability in absolute numbers is documented, and the consistency of regional patterns within cortical regions is demonstrated across multiple animals (n=3 per region). However, the lack of correlation between injection volume and terminal number (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D) suggests the variability may not be solely due to injection size.

results.result: The proportion of cortical input to the vermis was similar across cortical regions (~30%), with exceptions: V1 had very few vermal projections (14±1%), A1 showed strong vermal bias (47±7%), and AuD deviated from A1 without vermal bias. V1 and PPC showed larger proportions to vestibulocerebellum, with PPC showing equal proportions across all cerebellar subdivisions (hemispheres: 40±3%, vermis: 30±7%, vestibulocerebellum: 30±3%).
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C82 are supported by quantification data in Figure 3C showing the distribution across cerebellar divisions. The specific percentages are provided for each cortical region, and the patterns are consistent across animals within each group. The finding that PPC is unique in showing equal proportions across divisions (C82) is well-documented.

results.result: M1 injections resulted in terminals primarily in contralateral crus II, Sim, PM, and crus I, with highly symmetrical bilateral patterns. S1 injections resulted in terminals in contralateral crus I, PM, and Cop, with S1 being the only region with substantial Cop input (14±5%). S1 showed relatively high terminals in vermal lobule IV/V and was largely symmetrical except for Cop.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C89 are supported by quantification data in Figure 3D. The specific percentages and patterns are documented for both M1 and S1. The unique projection to Cop from S1 (C86) is well-quantified (14±5% vs <1.7% for other regions). The symmetry/asymmetry patterns (C84, C89) are demonstrated in the bilateral quantification.

results.result: PPC injections resulted in less laterality but substantial differences between ipsilateral and contralateral patterns. Contralaterally, PPC showed balanced projections to crus I (19±6%), lobules IV-VI (10±1%), and paraflocculus (19±6%). Ipsilaterally, crus I labeling was less prevalent (4±0.5%) but with larger proportions to vermal lobule VI (13±7%) and crus II (5±2%), resulting in the lowest laterality but least symmetrical terminal organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C94 are supported by quantification data in Figure 3D. The specific percentages for ipsilateral and contralateral projections are provided, and the differences between sides are clearly documented. The conclusion that PPC shows lowest laterality but least symmetry (C94) is a valid inference from the quantitative data.

results.result: V1 injections resulted in most terminals in contralateral PFl (44±5%), with ipsilateral PFl receiving less than a third of that (7±2%). Crus I was the only hemispheric region with substantial V1 labeling (16±6% contralateral). Vermal labeling was sparse but highly symmetric, with lobule VI most prominent (5±2%).
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 are supported by quantification data in Figure 3D. The specific percentages are provided for each region, and the patterns are consistent with the overall finding of V1 bias toward vestibulocerebellum (C80). The symmetry of vermal labeling (C98) is documented in the bilateral quantification.

results.result: A1 injections resulted in large proportions of terminals in vermis (lobules III: 9±5%, IV/V: 12±2%, VI: 8±2%) and fairly equal distribution in hemispheres (crus I: 8±1%, crus II: 7±1%). A1 was unique in showing similar proportions to cerebellar hemispheres bilaterally (ipsilateral: 18±2%, contralateral: 24±2%).
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 are supported by quantification data in Figure 3D. The specific percentages are provided for each lobule, and the unique bilateral pattern for A1 (C101) is well-documented. This finding is consistent with the overall vermal bias observed for A1 (C78) and the lack of direct pontine pathway (C4).

results.result: AuD injections resulted in prominent labeling in crus I (15±3%) and crus II (8±1%), followed by vermal lobules IV/V (7±0.4%) and VI (7±1%), with very few terminals in lobule III (0.9±0.1%). The pattern was highly symmetrical bilaterally despite slightly higher absolute numbers contralaterally.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C104 are supported by quantification data in Figure 3D. The specific percentages are provided, and the contrast with A1 (C103) is documented. The symmetrical pattern (C104) is consistent with the overall finding of less laterality for association cortices (C8).

results.result: Vermal lobules IV/V and VI together received 18.1% of ipsilateral and 17.7% of contralateral terminals. A notable scarcity of terminals was found in posterior vermis, especially lobule VII (1.2% ipsilateral, 0.4% contralateral), contrary to studies of pontocerebellar projections alone. The PFl received a large proportion of inputs (7.9% ipsilateral, 11.6% contralateral) considering its relatively smaller volume.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C110 are supported by quantification data in Figure 4A-B. The specific percentages are provided for each region. The scarcity in lobule VII (C109) is noted as contrary to previous studies, which is appropriately cited. The observation about PFl (C110) considers volume, which is a valid consideration for interpreting the data.

results.result: In cerebellar hemispheres, the highest density of terminals was from M1, especially ipsilaterally (Sim, crus I, crus II, PM, excluding Cop). Bilaterally, Cop had highest density from S1, with 96% of contralateral Cop terminals originating from S1. Vermal lobules had highest density from S1, except ipsilateral lobule VI (high M1) and posterior vermal regions IX-X.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 are supported by density calculations in Figure 4C and Supplementary file 1C. The density metric (terminals/mm³) appropriately accounts for volume differences between lobules. The finding that 96% of Cop terminals are from S1 (C114) is a striking result that is well-quantified.

results.result: The vestibulocerebellum had diverse cerebrocerebellar input. Bilaterally, PFl and Fl had highest density from S1 but substantial input from other regions. Lobules IX and X had sparse input, with IX showing proportionally large auditory input (A1, AuD) and X showing M1 representation. Most vestibulocerebellar regions (except PFl) had small terminal density, requiring caution in interpretation.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C121 are supported by quantification and density data in Figures 4A-C. The diversity of input (C116-C117) and specific patterns for lobules IX and X (C118) are documented. The methodological caution (C120-C121) about interpreting patterns in regions with low density is appropriate and demonstrates scientific rigor.

results.result: Retrograde tracing showed lobules IV/V and VI had relatively higher proportions of extra-pontine labeling (44% and 39%) compared to cerebellar hemispheres (17% and 21%). Lobule VII received pontocerebellar projections but proportionally few compared to other regions (52% pontine vs 48% extra-pontine), originating largely from lateral pons that receives RSC input.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C168 are supported by retrograde tracing data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 3. The specific percentages are provided for each region. The observation about lobule VII (C167-C168) is consistent with the finding of few cerebrocerebellar terminals to this region (C217) and suggests it may receive input from higher-order cortical areas.

results.result: AAV1.cre acts as a mono-trans-synaptic anterograde tracer that crosses a single functional synapse.
results.evaluation: Claim C26 is supported by citations to methodological papers (Zingg et al., 2017; Zingg et al., 2020). The mono-trans-synaptic nature is validated by the absence of labeling in granule cells and Purkinje cells (C65-C66), which would indicate higher-order transfer. The method is well-established in the cited literature.

results.result: Cerebrocerebellar mossy fiber terminal labeling was systematically present in the granule cell layer regardless of cortical origin. No AAV1.cre-induced tdTomato expression was found in granule cells or Purkinje cells, indicating the AAV construct did not transfer beyond mono-synaptic connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by experimental observations (Figure 1F) and citations to methodological papers. The absence of labeling in granule cells and Purkinje cells (C65) provides important validation that the tracing is limited to mono-trans-synaptic connections (C66), which is critical for interpreting the results.

results.result: Although M1 injections resulted in bilateral pontine labeling, the resulting mossy fiber terminals were still largely located in the contralateral cerebellum (74±2%).
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are supported by data in Figures 3B, 1E, 3D, and 1F. The observation that bilateral pontine labeling does not result in equal bilateral cerebellar labeling is interesting and suggests that the contralateral pontine cells project more extensively to the cerebellum or that pontocerebellar projections themselves are predominantly contralateral.

results.result: Sparse contralateral corticopontine projections are axon terminals for M1 projections but fibers of passage for all other cortical target regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C47 are inferred from the observation of labeled cells in contralateral pons after M1 injections (C43) but not after other cortical injections (C42). This is a reasonable inference from the data, as the presence of trans-synaptically labeled cells indicates functional synapses. The interpretation is consistent with previous findings in primates (C48).

results.result: The reticulotegmental nucleus is classified as a separate extra-pontine region in this study based on evidence that it plays different functional roles than basal pontine nuclei.
results.evaluation: Claim C53 is a methodological decision supported by citation (Cicirata et al., 2005). This classification choice is reasonable and transparent, allowing readers to understand how the data were categorized. The functional distinction is based on prior literature.

results.result: Labeled fibers were observed in both medial and inferior cerebellar peduncles, indicating disynaptic tracts projecting to the cerebellum from pontine regions and more caudal extra-pontine precerebellar nuclei, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C55 are supported by anatomical observations in Figure 2A. The inference about disynaptic tracts (C55) is reasonable based on the known anatomy of cerebellar peduncles: the middle peduncle carries pontocerebellar fibers and the inferior peduncle carries fibers from more caudal brainstem nuclei.

results.result: No labeled cells were observed from any target cortical region in the spinal or lateral vestibular nuclei, the external cuneate nucleus, or the inferior olive.
results.evaluation: Claim C57 is supported by experimental observations. This negative result is important for defining the boundaries of direct cortical projections to precerebellar nuclei. However, the observation of fibers/terminals in the inferior olive after S1 and M1 injections (C58-C59) suggests indirect pathways to this structure.

results.result: Sparse fibers were observed in the lateral cerebellar nucleus following S1 and M1 injections, likely from pontocerebellar collaterals.
results.evaluation: Claim C63 is supported by experimental observations and citations (Cicirata et al., 2005; Biswas et al., 2019). The interpretation that these are pontocerebellar collaterals is reasonable based on the cited literature showing that pontine neurons can send collaterals to cerebellar nuclei.

results.result: In PFl and lobule VI, pairwise distance between terminal locations was not significantly different between M1 and other cortical origins, but S1 terminals were more tightly clustered to each other in both regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C145 are supported by statistical analysis of spatial data in Figure 6B. The finding that S1 terminals are more clustered (C145) is consistent with the patchy distribution observed for S1 throughout the cerebellum (C146) and may reflect the somatotopic organization of S1 projections.

results.result: The pattern of S1 projections is in agreement with results from electrophysiological recordings in the PM in rats, demonstrating alternating patches of somatosensory responses to hindlimb/forelimb stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claim C148 is supported by citation to previous research (Shambes et al., 1978). This cross-validation with functional data from another species strengthens the interpretation of the anatomical findings. The agreement between anatomical and functional studies supports the biological relevance of the observed patterns.

results.result: Previous studies using single neuron tracing techniques have reported a comparable 67±7 (mice) and 46±9 (rats) mossy fiber terminals in the cerebellum per pontine projecting neuron.
results.evaluation: Claim C171 is supported by citations to previous research (Biswas et al., 2019; Na et al., 2019). The comparison with the current study's estimate of ~50 mossy fibers per precerebellar neuron (C170) shows good agreement with previous single-neuron tracing studies, providing validation of the quantification approach.

results.result: Following injections centered around hindlimb/forelimb regions in mice, a substantial caudal bias in the pontine nuclei was not found, as has previously been reported in rats. Whether this reflects a species difference requires finer detailed somatotopic mapping in mouse S1.
results.evaluation: Claims C175-C176 are supported by comparison with previous studies via citations (Leergaard et al., 2003; Odeh et al., 2005). The observation of a difference from rat studies (C175) is documented, and the acknowledgment that finer somatotopic mapping is needed (C176) is appropriate scientific caution. This represents a potential species difference that warrants further investigation.

results.result: Mossy fiber terminals were more biased to vermal regions after A1 injections and included more projections to the cerebellar hemispheres (especially crus I) after AuD injections.
results.evaluation: Claim C181 is supported by quantification data showing the different patterns for A1 (vermal bias, C78) versus AuD (hemispheric projections without vermal bias, C79). This observation is consistent with the finding that A1 lacks direct pontine projections (C4) while AuD has them (C33), suggesting different pathways may target different cerebellar regions.

results.result: The pattern of pontine cell labeling observed following AuD injections was topographically distinct from the location of labeled fibers after A1 injections.
results.evaluation: Claim C187 is supported by comparison of spatial patterns in the data. This observation argues against the interpretation that the fibers in the pons after A1 injections are terminals from trans-synaptically labeled secondary auditory cortex cells, supporting alternative explanations for the origin of these fibers (C37-C38).

results.result: Direct projections from the IC to dorsolateral regions of the pons were confirmed.
results.evaluation: Claim C189 is supported by experimental observations and citation (Caicedo and Herbert, 1993). This confirmation is important for supporting the proposed trisynaptic A1-IC-pontine-cerebellar pathway (C40) and provides anatomical evidence for one of the potential routes for A1 input to reach the cerebellum.

results.result: Anterograde labeling in the IC from auditory cortex was largely in the DCIC subregion, where corticocollicular projections have been suggested to play a modulatory role on auditory processing, compared to sharper frequency tuning in CIC.
results.evaluation: Claims C190-C192 are supported by experimental observations (C190) and citations to previous research (C191-C192). The observation that labeling is in DCIC rather than CIC is consistent with the modulatory role of corticocollicular projections and may have functional implications for the type of auditory information reaching the cerebellum.

results.result: A1 in mouse has been shown to be tonotopically organized, whereas the dorsal belt of auditory cortex is not, and auditory corticopontine projections in cats are also not tonotopically organized. Whether tonotopic organization is a determinant for auditory corticopontine projections requires further consideration.
results.evaluation: Claims C193-C195 are supported by citations to previous research. The speculation about whether tonotopic organization determines corticopontine projections (C195) is reasonable given the observations that A1 (tonotopic) lacks pontine projections while AuD (non-tonotopic) has them, and that auditory corticopontine projections in cats are not tonotopically organized.

results.result: The cochlear nuclear complex, which projects directly to pontine nuclei and cerebellum as mossy fibers, may serve as a disynaptic and potentially trisynaptic (via pontine nuclei) auditory cerebrocerebellar intermediate, which may be functionally relevant for temporal processing of auditory information.
results.evaluation: Claims C196-C198 are supported by citations to previous research showing the anatomical connections (C196). The speculation about the cochlear nucleus as an intermediate (C197) and its functional relevance for temporal processing (C198) is reasonable based on the known anatomy and function of this structure. However, these remain speculative interpretations that require further investigation (C199).

results.result: While the mono-trans-synaptic tracing does not permit precise segregation of pontine versus extra-pontine pathways, observations from retrograde tracing and fiber tracts suggest both pontine and extra-pontine nuclei act as sources of mossy fiber input through disynaptic cerebrocerebellar pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C201-C203 appropriately acknowledge the methodological limitation (C201) while drawing reasonable inferences from the combined data (C202-C203). The conclusion that both pontine and extra-pontine nuclei contribute to cerebellar input is supported by the retrograde tracing data (C159, C163) and the observation of fibers in both cerebellar peduncles (C54-C55).

results.result: Previous studies found that the majority of pontocerebellar mossy fibers terminate contralaterally. The current study found mono-trans-synaptically labeled mossy fibers from cerebral cortex project to varying degrees ipsilaterally and contralaterally. These projections can cross at the level of pontine nuclei or cerebellar peduncles, or both.
results.evaluation: Claims C207-C209 are supported by citation to previous research (C207) and quantification data from the current study (C208). The inference about crossing at different levels (C209) is reasonable and supported by citations to recent single-neuron tracing studies (Biswas et al., 2019; Na et al., 2019) showing both patterns.

results.result: Using retrograde rabies tracing, relatively large bilateral cerebrocerebellar pathways were found from orbitofrontal and retrosplenial cortical regions to posterior cerebellar cortex. This pattern suggests that information from 'higher-order' prefrontal and cortical association areas may have a more global effect on cerebellar processing than more targeted 'unisensory' or primary motor inputs, though broader functional implications remain to be determined.
results.evaluation: Claims C211-C213 are supported by citation to previous research (C211, Suzuki et al., 2012). The speculation about global versus targeted effects (C212) is a reasonable interpretation of the laterality patterns observed in the current study (C210) and the cited study. The acknowledgment that functional implications remain to be determined (C213) is appropriate scientific caution.

results.result: A relatively large number of labeled mossy fibers were found in lobules IV/V but few in posterior vermal regions including lobule VII. Lobule IV/V is functionally considered part of the spinocerebellum and implicated in motor function, but not traditionally described as receiving extensive pontocerebellar or cortical input. Recent studies have emphasized modulation by behavioral state and locomotive behaviors, with suggestions that predictive motor responses may carry a motor efference copy from higher cortical areas. The current results confirmed disynaptic cerebrocerebellar and direct pontocerebellar input to lobule IV/V in mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C217-C221 are supported by quantification data (C217), established knowledge (C218), and citations to recent research (C219-C220). The confirmation of cerebrocerebellar input to lobule IV/V (C221) provides anatomical support for the functional observations in recent studies, demonstrating good integration of the current findings with the broader literature.

results.result: Very few cerebrocerebellar terminals were observed in lobule VII, seemingly contradicting previous findings of large pontocerebellar pathways to this region. However, the results are in agreement with suggestions in other species that pontocerebellar inputs to lobule VII may relay cortical information of higher order than primary motor and sensory areas (retrosplenial cortex, prefrontal regions) or subcortical brain regions (superior colliculus, accessory optic system).
results.evaluation: Claims C222-C224 are supported by quantification data (C217, C222) and citations to previous research (C222-C224). The apparent contradiction with previous studies (C222) is resolved by considering that lobule VII may receive input from cortical areas not examined in the current study (C223-C224). This interpretation is supported by the retrograde tracing data showing pontine input to lobule VII originates from lateral pons that receives RSC input (C168).

results.result: The cerebral cortex and cerebellum both play important roles in sensorimotor processing, with connections forming one of the largest projection pathways in the brain that has undergone selective expansion across evolution. However, precise connections between these structures remain elusive due to their indirect nature and methodological limitations, with the precise routes for information flow remaining largely inferred.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C11-C21 represent background knowledge and motivation for the study, supported by citations to previous research and established understanding of the field. These claims appropriately set up the rationale for the current study by identifying gaps in knowledge (C2, C16, C17, C21) and methodological limitations (C17, C20) that the current work addresses.

results.result: The integration of multimodal inputs to the cerebellum is a fundamental operation that would allow for precise coordination of sensory-driven movements. While the potential for a single granule cell to receive multimodal input via descending motor cortex and ascending proprioceptive pathways has been shown in mice, the potential for co-innervation from various cortical areas spanning multiple modalities is unknown, even on the regional level, and has consequences for cerebro-cerebellar-cerebro feedback loops in learning and predictive motor control.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C25 represent theoretical background and identification of knowledge gaps that motivate the study. The theoretical statement about multimodal integration (C22) is supported by general knowledge and citation (C23). The identification of the knowledge gap (C24) and its functional implications (C25) appropriately set up the specific aims of the current study.

results.result: Previous anterograde tracer studies observed corticopontine fibers largely in ipsilateral pontine nuclei with relatively sparse contralateral labeling, but it was unclear if these sparse contralateral projections were fibers of passage or axon terminals. The existence of functional synapses for contralateral corticopontine projections was also reported in primates, exclusively after M1 injections.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C45, C48 are supported by citations to previous research. These claims provide important context for interpreting the current findings about bilateral M1 projections (C43, C46) and show that the current results in mice are consistent with findings in primates (C48).

results.result: There is controversy regarding the existence of direct cerebro-olivary connections in rodents, particularly originating from M1.
results.evaluation: Claim C61 is supported by citations to previous research showing conflicting results. This context is important for interpreting the current findings of fibers and terminals in the inferior olive after S1 and M1 injections (C58-C59) and the observation of labeled cells in matrix region x (C60), which together support disynaptic rather than direct input (C62).

results.result: Cerebellar lobules contain highly organized parasagittally oriented modules based on anatomical, physiological and molecular subdivisions. The parasagittal expression pattern of aldolase C is highly conserved across individuals.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C125 are based on established knowledge supported by citations. This background is important for understanding the approach used to align data across animals and examine the relationship between mossy fiber terminals and molecularly defined modules. The conservation of AldoC patterns (C125) is validated by the correlation analysis across animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1J).

results.result: The results do not preclude the existence of a finer-scale relationship between terminals and AldoC expression with respect to individual cerebrocerebellar pathways and/or in a lobule specific manner.
results.evaluation: Claim C158 is a cautionary statement about the interpretation of the results. This is appropriate scientific caution given that the terminals potentially relay through multiple precerebellar nuclei (as documented in Supplementary file 1B and Figure 2), and finer-scale relationships may exist that are not detected at the level of analysis performed.

results.result: The probability of double labeling was likely low due to the spatially restricted injection sites.
results.evaluation: Claim C162 is a methodological consideration that appropriately acknowledges a limitation of the dual injection experiments. The spatially restricted nature of the injections means that only a small subset of the total population of precerebellar neurons projecting to the injected cerebellar region would also receive input from the injected cortical region, making double labeling relatively rare.

results.result: Some differences in corticopontine organization may exist across species. There are substantial conflicting results in many species describing either the presence or absence of an A1-pontine pathway, and studies in mice have not been extensive.
results.evaluation: Claims C174, C182-C183 are supported by citations to previous research showing conflicting results across species. This context is important for interpreting the current finding of no A1-pontine pathway in mice (C184) and acknowledges the complexity of the literature on this topic.

results.result: Precerebellar nuclei may play an important functional role to relay/integrate multimodal information from the cerebral cortex to the cerebellum. The nature of relay versus integration of cortical signals along each of these precerebellar pathways will make for interesting future studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C204, C206 are speculative statements about functional implications and future research directions, supported by citations (C204). These are appropriate interpretations of the anatomical findings and identify important questions for future investigation. The distinction between relay and integration (C206) is a key functional question that cannot be answered by the anatomical data alone.

results.result: The cerebellar hemispheres as well as lobules VI and VII are traditionally described as cerebrocerebellar receiving areas.
results.evaluation: Claim C214 is based on established knowledge supported by citations. This traditional view provides important context for interpreting the current findings, which both confirm (cerebellar hemispheres as major target, C215) and challenge (few terminals in lobule VII, C217) aspects of this traditional understanding.

results.result: Spatial overlaps of cerebrocerebellar inputs constitute the fundamental anatomical basis for multimodal integration processes of cortical information at a modular and potentially cellular level.
results.evaluation: Claim C228 is a theoretical interpretation of the anatomical findings, supported by citation (Proville et al., 2014). This interpretation is reasonable given the documented spatial overlap of terminals from different cortical regions (C9, C126, C133, C225) and provides a framework for understanding the functional significance of the anatomical organization.

results.result: In vivo electrophysiological and imaging studies have shown that single granule cells can respond to multiple modalities in rat, mouse and mormyrid fish, with half of granular cells in crus I/II and vermal lobule VI responding to sensory stimuli and many showing responses to multiple modalities. However, in functional studies to date, the specific origin of mossy fiber inputs was either undetermined or from bottom-up brainstem centers, and in decerebrated cats granule cells respond to only one modality.
results.evaluation: Claims C229-C233 are supported by citations to previous research. This functional context is important for interpreting the anatomical findings of spatial overlap (C9, C225) and suggests that the potential for multimodal convergence of cerebrocerebellar inputs may be an important determinant of granule cell function (C234).

results.result: The potential for multimodal convergence of cerebrocerebellar inputs in the granule cell layer may be an important determinant of granule cell function. Alternatively, the majority of basic sensory information may be carried by ascending pathways and descending cerebrocerebellar pathways may be carrying action-related information from various cortical regions, including from primary sensory areas where motor behaviors influence sensory responses. The cerebellum may use these cortical signals in closed feedback loops to regulate and adjust ongoing predictive responses, as suggested by a feed forward model for motor control.
results.evaluation: Claims C234-C237 are speculative interpretations of the anatomical findings, supported by citations to previous research. These represent reasonable hypotheses about the functional significance of the observed anatomical organization. The alternative interpretations (C234 vs C235) appropriately acknowledge that the anatomical data alone cannot distinguish between different functional models.

results.result: Future studies examining the precise nature of information carried by cerebrocerebellar pathways will further elucidate functional influence of cerebral cortex on cerebellar processing. Assessing full functional contribution will require advanced anatomical delineation of polysynaptic circuits combined with simultaneous observation and circuit manipulation in behaving animals. Mouse models provide many advantages due to access to advanced genetic tools and increasingly complex behavioral paradigms. The results demonstrate conserved principles of organization between mice and other mammalian species and provide foundational insight into diversity and potential for spatial multimodal convergence within cerebrocerebellar pathways in mice, which will guide future research to delineate the precise nature of sensorimotor integration at multiple circuit levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C238-C243 represent statements about future research directions and the impact of the current work. These are appropriate conclusions that identify important next steps (C238-C239), acknowledge the advantages of the mouse model (C240), and summarize the contributions of the current study (C241-C243). The claims about conserved principles (C241) are supported by the comparisons with previous studies in other species throughout the manuscript.
